Charuma is a trick-taking game with a fast bidding phase and a partially closed hand. The card game has only two suit colours (blue and red). The cards are numbered from 1 (Ace) to 10, and there are two copies of each card.
In a game of Charuma, each player has two cards in their hand, which they do not show to the other players. The rest of their hand is placed on the table in front of them, face up.

At the start of each round, you must use your victory points to buy these visible cards in a quick bidding phase based on the cards you have in your hand, your position in the turn order, and the other cards you see on the table. It is up to you to decide which hand is best for you and how much you are willing to pay to get it.
Once the auction is over, the game phase begins. The first player starts the first trick by playing 1 or 2 cards. If you play 2 cards, you must play a pair (two-coloured or single-coloured), i.e. 2 cards of the same value.
Charuma offers some fairly simple tricks to disrupt the natural value of the cards and ensure that it is not always the 10 that wins the trick:
- If two identical cards are in a trick, the second card played is stronger than the first. This will occasionally prompt you to lose the hand to reverse the cards' value.
- If you have the suit requested visible in your hand, you must play it. If you do not have the requested suit visible in your hand, or if you have it but it is hidden, you are not obliged to play it. You must discard the number of cards requested, but you cannot win the trick.
- If an ace and a 10 of the same suit are in the same trick, then the ace is not worth 1, but, in this case and only in this case, it beats the 10.
If you open a trick with a pair of cards (e.g. two suits), you force your opponents to play pairs (in this case, two suits). The three rules above apply.
If a player does not have a two-colour pair, they discard two cards without any colour restrictions but cannot win the trick.A pair 2 reds cards can therefore beat a nine and a ten.
Each trick earns you 1 point, or 2 points if it is an open trick with a pair (2 cards per player). Each Ace earns you a bonus of 1 point, and the last trick earns you another bonus of 2 points. 
Charuma thus encourages you to take risks with the cards you keep for the end of the round. There are quite a few points to be earned, but you don't know whether to keep blue, red, or a specific combination.
All this means that each bidding phase requires you to make choices and manage your victory points throughout the game.
Charuma is a trick-taking game that involves analysis, control, and a degree of risk-taking. It's up to you to find or place the cursor between these different factors.

—description from the publisher
community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] It's not bad, though also feels too restrictive most of the time. It most reminds me of Dog Tag Trick with its card combos (and reward for the last trick), but that game felt so open with possibilities and combinations. Here it's heavily restricted by suits, but hands are too small to do much with them. Most of the game is in bidding for public hands, but since there's so few hidden cards that means it's not as psychological as I hoped. Plus the needlessly complex rules for what's legal to play, ech.

[Rating: 3/10] It has too many problems.   Going second or third is terrible, and since the player with the lowest points always start a round first, you'll always be at a disadvantage if you start after them.  With 8 cards out in a 4 player game, it's far too unpredictable, and with 2 blind cards, if you draw well, you'll probably have a huge advantage.  And worst of all, since most cards are out in the open, you expect people to play in a way (optimally) and when they do not, your whole game just crashes and burns.  Just play a normal trick-taking game.

[Rating: 3/10] A trick taking game where each round, players start with 2 face down cards and draft a row of face up cards with points. Once all players gain a row, players play 1 or 2 cards, higher is better, with cards played that can not play the correct meld (color or pair) will not win. A single ace beats a single 10, likewise with pairs. Each trick won or an ace is 1 point. Once a certain number of points is gained, the player with the most points wins.

[Rating: 5/10] Not sure what the appeal is of playing your cards with an open hand.   Players bid on a set of 6 visible cards using their victory points and get two hidden cards.  Then you play a pretty basic trick taking game where each trick is worth a point and aces are worth a point.  You can play a duo of cards as well and get two points for those.  Everyone can see 6 of your 8 cards and each hand goes pretty much just like you think.

Les différentes manches nous ont laissé perplexes, car sans réel contrôle sur le jeu. Malgré nos 2 cartes cachées, notre jeu visible de tous ne nous a pas paru être challengeant, ni même tout simplement intéressant. Jeu moche et peu convainquant.
